The purchase consideration includes payment for the following as well: (1) ₹ 2 crores for obtaining the skilled staff at LB LLP. (2) ₹ 2 crores by way of payment towards “Non-compete fee” so as to restrict LB LLP to compete in the same line of business for next 5 years. However, items (1) and (2) are not forming part of the ₹ 11 crores fair value of net assets acquired. Hope this provides you with dall the details required to account for this acquisition. Stefan. |  |


            
            

| I. | Multiple Choice Questions |
| --- | --- |


            

2.1 Which of the following statements is correct in respect of TDS deducted on the variable pay of the partners?


            

(A) TDS on variable pay is being deducted correctly at the time of payment to the partner that is in June of the next financial year.


            

(B) TDS on variable pay is being deducted at the correct rate at the time of payment to the partner.


            

(C) TDS on variable pay is being deducted incorrectly as it should be done @ 5% and not 15%.


            

(D) TDS on variable pay is being deducted incorrectly as it should be done @ 10% and at the time of crediting such sum to the capital account of the partner.


            

2.2 Is the claim of Smt. Jaya Kulkarni, the legal representative of Late CA. Atul Kulkarni justified?


            

(A) Yes, the claim of Smt. Jaya Kulkarni is justified as CA. Atul Kulkarni was a partner at MP LLP and therefore is entitled to receive a share in the firm’s profits as long as it exists.


            

(B) Yes, the claim of Smt. Jaya Kulkarni is justified but only if the partnership deed of MP LLP provides for such an event.


            

(C) No, the claim of Smt. Jaya Kulkarni is not justified as the she is not a partner at MP LLP and therefore possesses no rights to stake a claim on its profits.


            

(D) No, the claim of Smt. Jaya Kulkarni is not justified as MP LLP dissolves immediately on the demise of its partner CA. Atul Kulkarni.


            

2.3 How would you interpret the resource utilization at MP LLP?


            

(A) Resource utilization in the most optimal in the accounting services


            

(B) Resource utilization in the most optimal in the audit services


            

(C) Resource utilization in the most optimal in the tax services


            

(D) Resource utilization in the most optimal in the business advisory services


            

2.4 Based on the results and determinants, which of the following has the most promising contribution for future growth of the firm’s business?


            

(A) Accounting service


            

(B) Audit service


            

(C) Tax consulting service


            

(D) Business advisory service


            

2.5 Which of the following shows that MP LLP has flexibility and innovation in its operations?


            

(A) Audit services contribute highest revenue for the firm


            

(B) Accounting services has revenue growth of 2% over the previous year


            

(C) Tax consultancy has the highest customer rating among the traditional legacy services offered by the firm excluding business advisory services, which has been recently introduced.


            

(D) Business advisory services has 40% market share of the industry for that service


            

**(5 × 2 = 10 Marks)**


            

| II. | Descriptive Questions |
| --- | --- |


            

2.6 Using Fitzgerald and Moon’s Building Block Model, critically evaluate the performance management framework of MP LLP by identifying one flaw in its Standards and one flaw in its Reward Structure. Suggest strategic recommendations for both.


            

**(4 Marks)**


            

2.7 Advise Sachin Nadkari to determine any intangible assets arising from the acquisition of LB LLP and how they need to be accounted for.


            

**(5 Marks)**


            

2.8 Evaluate the correctness of Sachin Nadkarni’s claim that there is no contravention relating to invoicing of HR and IT services as laid down in the provisions of the GST law.


         

**(6 Marks)**
explanation:
| Answer-2 |
| --- |

| I. | Answers to the Multiple Choice Questions |
| --- | --- |


           

**2.1 Option (D)** TDS on variable pay is being deducted incorrectly as it should be done @ 10% and at the time of crediting such sum to the capital account of the partner.


           

**Reason:** As per section 194T of the Income Tax Act, 1961 TDS on payments to partners in the form of salary, remuneration, commission, bonus or interest should be made at the time of crediting the account of the partner (including the capital account) or at the time of payment, whichever is earlier. The applicable rate is 10%. Here, MP LLP is crediting the variable pay to the partner’s capital account as and when it accrues. The actual payment is made on a later date in June of the next financial year. Therefore, MP LLP has to deduct TDS @ 10% of such variable pay when the partner’s capital account is credited with such amount and not at the time of its payment in June next year.


           

**2.2 Option (B)** Yes, the claim of Smt. Jaya Kulkarni is justified but only if the partnership deed of MP LLP provides for such an event.


           

**Reason:** In interpreting Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, the Code of Ethics stipulates that sharing of fees or profits with the legal representative (such as a widow) of a deceased partner is permissible only if the partnership agreement explicitly contains such provisions that entitles them to such payments. Therefore, the claim of Smt. Jaya Kulkarni is justified but only if the partnership deed of MP LLP provides for such an event.


           

**2.3 Option (D)** Resource utilization in the most optimal in the business advisory services.


           

**Reason:** Resource utilization is determines future success. In the given case, it is m ost optimal in the business advisory services. The quality of service, the net profit ratio are the highest as compared to other domains. It also has a sizable market share in this domain.


           

**2.4 Option (D)** Business advisory service.


           

**Reason:** It has the highest customer satisfaction rating. It also has a high margin since the net profit ratio is the highest among all the revenue streams for the firm. It also has a sizable share of the industry’s advisory business.


           

**2.5 Option (D)** Business advisory services has 40% market share of the industry for that service.


           

**Reason:** A slowdown in the economy has businesses are entering into either internal/ external reconstruction. Here MP LLP has a 40% market share of this domain service, with a high net profit margin and high customer satisfaction rating. These have been achieved within just 1 year of introduction of this service. This shows that MP LLP has adapted to the needs changing economic environment (flexibility) and has innovated to offer these services to its clients.


           

| II. | Answers to the Descriptive Questions |
| --- | --- |


           

**2.6** According to Fitzgerald and Moon’s Building Block Model, standards are the measures used to evaluate performance. They are the Key Performance Indicators (KPI) that should have characteristics like (1) equity (2) ownership and (3) achievable to make them just and fair while evaluating performance.


           

MP LLP has established an across-the-board 10% revenue growth target for all service segments. According to the Building Block Model, performance standards must possess equity, meaning they should be equally challenging and fair for all units. This uniform target lacks equity. The Business Advisory segment grew at 18% last year, while tax advisory grew at 10%. These segments operate in a high-demand market, making a 10% target easily achievable. Conversely, the Accounting segment only grew at 2%, while audit grew at 6% last year. These segments operate within a highly mature and stagnant market environment, making a 10% target realistically impossible to attain.


           

Partners must transition to localized, realistic benchmarks that factor in the distinct market life cycles and growth potentials of individual segments. Dimensions of performance that are defined and measured using these standards impacts employee motivation and drives success.


           

According to Fitzgerald and Moon’s Building Block Model, clear and controllable rewards ensure that employees are motivated to the standards of performance set by the organization.


           

Rewards should possess the following characteristics: (1) Motivation (2) Clarity and (3) Controllability.


           

MP LLP has an HR policy that states that non-partners get a variable pay component that in addition to individual and team performance, is also significantly dependent on whether the firm meets its target profits for the year. In addition to many other internal and external factors, overall firm profit depends on partners’ decisions, economic conditions etc. which are not in the control of non-partners. Therefore, linking variable pay to such factors beyond the control of non-partners will demotivate employees. Rewards must to linked to factors that the employees can actually influence and control. Under the Building Block Model, staff must only be penalized or rewarded based on outcomes they can directly influence. It is mentioned in the case study that t here have been instances when a good performer who is part of a well performing team did not any significant variable pay on account of the firm not meeting its profit targets. Denying bonuses to good performers due to macro failures severely drives down motivation.


           

MP LLP should decouple determination of non-partner variable pay to be slightly less significantly dependent on firm-level targets, linking incentives more directly to individual performance appraisals and immediate team metrics. While the firm’s overall profits would indeed impact the variable pay of employees, it should be more significantly linked to the variable pay of partners who are the decision makers that drive the firm’s profitability and less so to the variable pay of non-partners who do not have the decisions making power relating to the firm’s operations.


           

In conclusion, to ensure long-term operational harmony, MP LLP must align its lagging Results (financial numbers) with upstream Determinants (employee motivation and service quality). Fixing structural issues around fairness and control ensures that high - growth segments stay incentivized while mature departments do not feel penalized by unachievable goals.


           

**2.7** Ind AS 38 covers accounting for intangible assets. Non-compete fees represents a contractual right that is separable from goodwill. Here, the fair value of the non-compete fees is reliably measured. Therefore, MP LLP should recognize an intangible asset in respect of the ₹2 crores consideration paid towards “Non compete Fees”.


           

However, amount paid for obtaining skilled staff amounting to ₹2 crores does not meet the definition of an intangible asset since MP LLP has not established any right over the resource and the same should be expensed. The entity has insufficient control over the expected future economic benefits arising from the team of skilled staff.


           

Therefore, ₹ 2 crores paid towards non- compete fee will be recognized separately as an intangible asset, whereas the amount paid for obtaining skilled staff does not meet the recognition criteria for being identified as a separate intangible asset and hence will be recognised separately. However, since it is acquired as part of a business combination, it forms part of the goodwill recognized at the acquisition date. The value of goodwill will be ₹ 2 crores, as calculated below:


           

Goodwill = Purchase consideration ( ₹ 15 crores) - Fair value of assets acquired ( ₹ 11 crores) - Non-compete fees ( ₹ 2 crores) = ₹ 2 crores


           

**2.8** Where there is supply of goods or service between distinct entities like the Head Office and its branches, they are considered taxable supply under the cross-charge mechanism of the CGST Act, 2017 [Section 7(1)(c) of the CGST Act, 2017]. The head office provides internal services like HR and IT to its branches, which are taxable services falling under this framework.


           

The value of supply of services made by the head office to its branches needs to be determined as per rule 28 of the CGST Rules, 2017 read with section 15(4) of the CGST Act, 2017. As per rule 28(a) of the CGST Rules, 2017 , the value of supply between distinct persons shall be the Open Market Value (OMV) of such supply. Where the recipient is eligible for full ITC, the value declared in the invoice shall be deemed to be the OMV of the services. (second proviso to rule 28).


           

Accordingly, in respect of supply of services by head office to branch offices, in cases where full ITC is available to a branch office, the value declared on the invoice by the head office to the said branch office in respect of the said supply shall be deemed to be the OMV of such services. This is irrespective of whether cost of any particular component of such services, like employee costs etc. has been included or not in the value of the services in the invoice. Therefore, where the invoice is issued, the open market value is the value declared in the invoice.


           

Further, in such cases where full ITC is available to the recipient, if HO has not issued a tax invoice to the BO in respect of any particular services being rendered by HO to the said BO, the value of such services may be deemed to be declared as Nil by HO to BO, and may be deemed as OMV in terms of second proviso to rule 28.


           

(1) In view of the above explanation, in case of HR services, the notional value of ₹ 50,000 per month per branch as raised by the HO in the GST tax invoice will be considered as the open market value. Therefore, the contention of the GST authorities that suggests that OMV declared in the invoice has to necessarily based on the open market value of similar services provided by third party vendors is incorrect.


           

Further the law states that in cases where full ITC is available to the recipient, if the head office has not issued a tax invoice to the branch office in respect of any particular service being rendered by the head office to the branch office, the value of such services may be deemed to be declared as Nil by head office to branch office. This will be deemed as the OMV in terms of the second proviso to rule 28. Therefore, where invoice is not issued, value of supply which is also the OMV will be considered NIL.


           

(2) In case of IT services, no invoice is being raised despite the services being provided by the HO to the branches. In its tax filings, MP LLP has been considering the OMV for these services to be NIL. This is the correct approach. Although these services have an open market value (OMV), in view of the above explanation, where no invoice is raised, the OMV will be deemed to be nil in terms of the second proviso to rule 28.


           

It can therefore be concluded that Sachin Nadkari is correct in contending that the firm is complying with the provisions of the GST Law in both cases.

| Dynamic Infra Engineering Limited (DIEL) is a large multi-national, listed company in India. DIEL has a tremendous track record of showing consistent business growth and is one of the key companies closely monitored by the equity analysts, PE investors, mutual funds and other stakeholders. You as a dynamic Chartered Accountant possessing inherent qualities viz. clarity of thought on the technical aspects of financial reporting, strategic financial management, cost and management accounting and legal compliances of various corporate and economic l aws have recently joined DIEL as its Vice President (Finance). Upon assuming your portfolio in the Company, the top management has clearly defined the role you need to play, given the multiple challenges impacting the organization. Therefore, timing of your entry in the company has become very crucial. The top management is scheduled to meet on 15th January 2027 wherein, several issues are likely to be discussed with you seeking your professional inputs and guidance. Despite its consistent growth, DIEL operates in an increasingly dynamic business environment characterised by rapid digitalisation, evolving regulatory and sustainability expectations, changing investor priorities and intensifying competitive pressures. The top management is deliberating whether the company should continue to rely substantially on its existing business model and capabilities or invest in developing and strengthening new capabilities to sustain its competitive position and long-term growth. One of the Indian subsidiaries of DIEL namely `Blue Metal Infra Engineering Limited` (BMIEL) is engaged in the business of building highway projects in India. It has borrowed US $ 200 million from a financial institution (FI) resident in US to invest in one of its ongoing buildings of highway projects in India. The rate of interest charged is 3% per annum. The US $ may be assumed ₹ 80. The top management wants to understand whether the income of the non-resident Fl is deemed to accrue or arise in India and the legal position in case the money is invested in one of its ongoing projects in Singapore. DIEL has incurred the following transactions for acquiring Plant "X` in part exchange of an old Plant Y. | (₹ in Lakhs) |
| --- | --- |
| Sale of scrap from the old site | 10 |
| Cost of construction of new site | 480 |
| Fair value of the old Plant Y, at which the supplier of the new Plant X has agreed to take it | 26 |
| The cash price paid to supplier for new Plant X | 320 |
| The carrying amount of old Plant Y | 10 |
| The present value of estimated dismantling cost of the site at the end of its useful life | 16 |

**3.8** The **McKinsey 7S Framework** suggests that successful strategic change requires alignment among seven interdependent organisational elements. In the case of DIEL, merely changing its strategy would not be sufficient; the other organisational elements must also be aligned with the changing business environment.


           

**Strategy:** DIEL should reassess its existing strategy in light of rapid digitalisation, sustainability requirements, regulatory developments, changing investor expectations and competitive pressures. It should formulate strategies that strengthen its long-term competitiveness rather than relying solely on its past record of growth.


           

**Structure:** The organisational structure should support the new strategic direction. DIEL may need greater coordination across finance, technology, operations, sustainability, risk and compliance functions and clearly defined responsibilities for implementing strategic initiatives across its multinational operations.


           

**Systems:** DIEL should strengthen its systems and processes relating to financial reporting, performance measurement, risk management, regulatory compliance, digital technologies and sustainability reporting. Appropriate information systems should provide management with timely information for strategic decision-making.


           

**Skills:** The Company should identify capability gaps and develop skills required for the emerging business environment. Particular emphasis may be placed on digital and analytical capabilities, strategic financial management, sustainability, risk management and regulatory competencies.


           

**Staff:** DIEL should ensure that it has people with the appropriate competencies to execute its strategy. This may require recruitment of specialised talent, reskilling and upskilling existing employees, leadership development and appropriate deployment of personnel across functions and subsidiaries.


           

**Style:** The leadership style should encourage innovation, adaptability, collaboration and accountability. The top management should actively support strategic transformation and promote timely decision-making in response to changes in the external environment.


           

**Shared Values:** DIEL`s shared values should provide the foundation for the other six elements. Values such as integrity, sustainable growth, innovation, stakeholder orientation and professional excellence should be embedded throughout the organisation and reflected in strategic and operational decisions.


           

**Conclusion**


           

DIEL should therefore adopt an **integrated approach to strategic change by ensuring alignment among all seven elements of the McKinsey 7S Framework**. Alignment of its strategy, structure, systems, skills, staff, style and shared values would enable DIEL to develop the organisational capabilities required to respond effectively to environmental changes and sustain its long-term competitive position.

For normal goods and services: 9 months from the date of export.


           

**Where an exporter receives advance payment (with or without interest), from a buyer / third party** named in the export declaration made by the exporter, outside India, the exporter shall be under an obligation to ensure that –


           

The shipment of goods is made within one year from the date of receipt of advance payment.


           

In case of **full conversion of ECB into equity**, the reporting to the Reserve Bank will be as under:


           

the entire portion is to be reported in **Form FC-GPR, while reporting to DSIM in Form ECB 2** Return should be done with remarks "ECB fully converted to equity". **Subsequent filing of Form ECB 2 Return is not required.**


           

**Limit for financial commitment** - The total financial commitment made by an Indian entity in all the foreign entities taken together at the time of undertaking such commitment shall not exceed **400 percent of its net worth as on the date of the last audited balance sheet** or as directed by the Reserve Bank, in consultation with Central Government from time to time.


           

**4.8 Checklist for documentary evidence to be submitted:**


           

A statement containing:


           
            
- 
             

number and date of export invoices along with copy of such Invoices,


            
            
- 
             

the number and date of shipping bills or bills of export along with copy of such shipping bills or bills of export,


            
            
- 
             

the number and date of Bank Realisation Certificate (BRC) or Foreign Inward Remittance Certificate (FIRC) in respect of such shipping bills or bills of export along with copy of such BRC / FlRC.


            
            
- 
             

the details of:


            
           
           

✓ refund already sanctioned,


           

✓ the number and date of relevant supplementary invoices or debit note issued subsequent to the upward revision in prices along with copy of such supplementary invoices/debit notes.


           
            
- 
             

the details of: 


             
              
               

payment of additional amount of IGST,


              
              
- 
               

proof of payment of such additional amount of integrated tax and interest paid thereon,


              
              
- 
               

number and date of FIRC in respect of additional FOREX received in respect of upward revision in price of exports along with copy of such FIRC.


              
             
            
           
           

**Certificate issued by a practicing-chartered accountant or a cost accountant** to the effect that the said additional FOREX remittance is on account of such upward revision in price of the goods subsequent to exports.


           

**Copy of contract or other documents, as applicable** .


           

A reconciliation statement reconciling the value of supplies declared in supplementary invoices, debit notes or credit notes issued along with relevant details of BRC or FIRC.

title: Integrated Business Solutions - Chapter 6 (4, 25M)

question:
| Background You are a Chartered Accountant, possessing hands on rich experience of more than a decade in providing professional advice on a diverse range of businesses. You are a unique individual known for making rational and correct judgements about data and numbers, possess the ability to identify and discover the potential solutions, assess alternatives and finally select/execute best solutions to fix the issue. Recently, you have joined as a partner in an established firm of Chartered Accountants based out of Chennai. Immediately on assuming your mantle, you were made in-charge of conducting the statutory audit of `Global Trends Limited` (GTL), located at Manaser, North India, a Company that operates a vast retail network, providing consumers with a wide range of fashionable apparel options. GTL`s vision is to emerge as a trusted and leading fashion retail brand by delivering contemporary, high-quality and accessible fashion while creating sustainable value for its stakeholders. In pursuit of this vision, its mission is to provide customers with fashionable, quality and value-driven apparel through an extensive retail network, supported by operational excellence, responsible business practices, innovation and a strong commitment to customer satisfaction. The Audit firm`s senior Partner, CA. N Natrajan has allocated to you to conduct the audit. The senior partner is very close to the family which owns the Company and you strongly believe that this is at least part of the reason why the Company decided to appoint your audit firm. The CFO of the Company made available to you the Annual Reports of the last five years and the draft summary of management prepared financial statements for the F.Y. 2025 -26. Before the commencement of the audit, you reviewed the Company`s audited financi al statements and accounts of the previous year. You noticed that the Auditors Report of the previous statutory auditor was qualified due to departure from Ind AS 2 on `Inventories’ wherein the management has not stated the inventories at lower of cost and net realizable value but has stated them solely at cost. At this juncture, you wished that you had access to the working papers of the previous auditors but you were informed that it was not possible. All said and done, you made a detailed audit program and deputed your audit team to look meticulously into every material aspect and conduct the audit from the propriety angle. You also instructed that all observations made by the audit team would be reviewed by you with proper assessments to ensure that the financial statements reflect a true and fair view. Your audit team has summarized the following items which are open and are pending to be dealt within the financial statements for your consideration: The Company has recognized deferred tax asset on the carried forward business losses. The Management do not foresee any future profits in the next couple of years. However, the Management expects confirmed orders after a couple of years. The amount of Cash and Cash Equivalents as at 01-04-2025 (excluding restricted cash and bank balances) was ₹40 lakh. The aggregate amount of Cash Flows during the FY 2025-26 from Operating, Investing and Financing Activities was ₹ 250 lakh. The amount of restricted bank balances as at 01-04-2025 and 31-03-2026 was ₹ 150 lakh and the Company does not believe the same as qualifying for disclosure under Cash and Cash Equivalents. As at 31-03-2026, the off Balance Sheet exposure in the form of Contingent Liabilities to the extent not paid and not provided for is ₹ 125 lakh. There was no disclosure of outstanding Letter of Credits (LCs) amounting to ₹ 60 lakh, opened for import of certain assets from Turkey under Contingent Liabilities in the financials prepared by the Company. The Company is liable to pay ₹ 5 lakh under protest against certain tax claims under dispute where the Company believes it has a fair chance of favourable orders and hence not provided in the financial statements nor was it disclosed as Contingent Liabilities. During the discussions, the Company has also mentioned that since they have not provided for the same, this would not be an item in the Companies (Auditor`s Report) Order 2020 (CARO, 2020) reporting by the Statutory Auditors as disputed dues. Sosmitha International Inc. has served a legal notice on the Company claiming ₹ 300 lakh for patent infringement and the Company has challenged the notice through its legal counsel. In this regard, an Independent legal opinion obtained suggests that the possibility of a cash outflow is more likely than not under the existing legal framework / available evidences as provided to the legal counsel. An amount of ₹ 125 lakh towards accrual of certain liabilities relating to refurbishment of certain spares meant for a specialized operating machine is yet to be made. The spares for refurbishment/receipt of spares were sent in March, 2026. Completion of the refurbishment/ receipt of spares by the Company is expected only in March, 2027. The amount of expected credit loss for doubtful receivables pending to be accounted as at 31 st March, 2026 is ₹ 105 lakh and the Company intend to account it proportionately on a straight line basis over the calendar year 2026 to spread the impact for the same. Further, no `Expected Credit Loss` (ECL) provision is considered for the `Retention Receivables` under the contract terms, which, if determined, would be ₹ 75 lakh as at 31st March, 2026. Other Inputs for Management Decision Making: GTL submitted a credit proposal to SCB Bank Limited for sanction of a Term Loan of ₹ 150 crore required for procuring and installing a latest Plant and Machinery for their upcoming project. Based on the application, SCB Bank Limited approached Ms. `C`, a Chartered Accountant, a friend of yours who is not associated with the Audit firm to investigate the profitability of the business for judging the accuracy of the schedule of repayment furnished by GTL as well as the value of the security in the form of assets of the business already possessed and those which will be created out of the loan. One of the associate companies of GTL is Nahar Hotels and Resorts Limited (NHR), which is engaged in the business of owning, operating and managing hotels during the previous year 2025-26. The tips are paid by the guests by way of charge to the Credit Cards, UPI or Net Banking in the bills. The Company disburses the same to the employees at periodic intervals. As of 31st March 2026, NHR has a share capital of ₹5 crores; reserves and surplus of ₹4 crores; long term debt of ₹ 16 crores; trade payables of ₹0.2 crores. NHR has demonstrated strong financial performance by achieving a profit before interest and tax (PBIT) of ₹9 crores; Interest paid for the financial year is ₹ 1.12 crores. The corporate tax rate is 30%; the cost of equity is 12.50% and the cost of debt is 4.9%. To effectively evaluate the company`s financial performance and make informed investment decisions, NHR utilizes the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) as a key metric. At all times, the management wishes to keep the average cost of financing the company`s operations across all sources of capital (debt and equity) to be below 10%. I. | Multiple Choice Questions |
| --- | --- |


            

[Please provide the correct option to the following questions].


            

5.1 The Company has recognized Deferred Tax Asset on the carried forward business losses. Do you think that this treatment is appropriate with reference to the relevant Ind AS?


            

(A) No, as it is not in compliance with the relevant Ind AS.


            

(B) Yes, as it is not only based on Management Assessment but also in compliance with the relevant Ind AS.


            

(C) Yes, as there are convincing evidences available.


            

(D) It depends on the decision to be taken by the Management if there is a probable merger with other entity.


            

5.2 What shall be amount of Cash and Cash Equivalent to be shown in the Cash Flow Statement as at 31st March, 2026 (₹ In Lakh)?


            

(A) 400


            

(B) 190


            

(C) 290


            

(D) 440


            

5.3 State the total amount of Contingent Liabilities of GTL as at 31st March, 2026. (₹ In Lakh)


            

(A) 130


            

(B) 315


            

(C) 390


            

(D) 430


            

5.4 With reference to the legal notice served by Sosmitha International Inc. on GTL for alleged patent infringement, which of the following statements BEST describes the strategic significance of a patent as a source of competitive advantage?


            

(A) A patent provides an organisation with an indefinite legal monopoly over an innovation, thereby ensuring sustainable competitive advantage.


            

(B) A patent provides legally enforceable protection for a specified period, which may enable an organisation to protect its innovation and derive economic benefits from it; however, such protection by itself does not necessarily ensure sustainable competitive advantage.


            

(C) A patent ensures competitive advantage only when competitors are completely prevented from developing alternative or substitute technologies.


            

(D) A patent automatically creates a sustainable competitive advantage because the patented resource necessarily satisfies all the criteria of value, rarity, inimitability and non-substitutability.


            

5.5 Expected Credit Loss Provisioning (ECL) is not required for Retention Receivables arising out of contract terms. The said statement is:


            

(A) Incorrect, since it is a financial asset/contract asset.


            

(B) Correct, in view of it being a contract asset.


            

(C) Correct, it all depends upon the general circumstances and facts.


            

(D) Incorrect, ECL is not applicable to Textile Companies.


            

**(5 × 2 = 10 Marks)**


            

| II. | Descriptive Questions |
| --- | --- |


            

5.6 In respect of the credit proposal submitted by GTL to SCB Bank Limited for sanction of a Term Loan of ₹ 150 crore required for procuring and installing a latest Plant and Machinery for their upcoming project, elucidate the steps that should be taken by Ms. C, Chartered Accountant to fulfill the requirements of SCB Bank Limited in this regard.


            

**(6 Marks)**


            

5.7 Explain with reasons whether the Company is responsible for deducting tax at source from disbursement of tips to its employees?


            

**(4 Marks)**


            

5.8 Evaluate NHR’s financial performance based on the given data.


         

**(5 Marks)**
explanation:
| Answer-5 |
| --- |

| I. | Answers to the Multiple Choice Questions |
| --- | --- |


           

**5.1 Option (A)** No, as it is not in compliance with the relevant Ind AS.


           

**Reason:** Ind AS 12 on “Income Taxes”, require exercise of prudence while recognizing tax assets and required only probable existence of taxable profit against which deductible temporary differences can be utilized. Ind AS 12 is more realistic focusing only on probable existence of taxable profits. Ind AS 12 moves to exercise caution only in case of unused tax losses, where it specifies that deferred tax asset arising from unused tax losses or tax credits can be recognized only to the extent that the entity has sufficient temporary differences of there is convincing other evidence that sufficient taxable profit will be available against which the unused tax losses or unused tax credits can be utilized by the entity. Considering that there is no such convincing evidence available in this case, deferred tax asset should not be recognized.


           

**5.2 Option (C)** 290


           

**Reason:** According to Ind AS 7, Statement of Cash Flows, cash and cash equivalents are defined as short term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and which are subject to insignificant risk of changes in value. In this case, opening cash and cash equivalents has been given as ₹ 40 Lakhs and this excludes the amount of bank balances that are restricted. The aggregate of the amount of cash flows during the financial year from operating, investing and financing activities is ₹ 250 lakhs. Since there is no movement in the opening and closing restricted cash balance, it does not impact net cash flows for the year. Accordingly, the closing cash and cash equivalents as at 31 March 2026 is ₹ 290 lakhs (₹ 40 lakhs plus ₹ 250 lakhs.)


           

**5.3 Option (A)** 130 Lakhs.


           

**Reason:** Ind AS 37 on ‘Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets’ defines contingent liability as a possible obligation that arises from past events and the existence of which will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more of the uncertain future events not wholly within the control of the entity or a presents obligation that arises from past events but is not recognized because (i) it is not probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation; or (ii) a reliable estimate of the amount of obligation cannot be made.


           

As per the facts of the case study:


           

The Company currently has disclosed ₹ 125 lakhs as contingent liabilities.


           

LCs opened for imports – is not a past or present obligation and it arises only in the future bases on when the vendor supplies the goods. Hence, an LC is not a contingent liability.


           

In respect of the tax liable to be paid of ₹ 5 lakhs, whilst the company believes it has a fair chance, it is a possible obligation the outcome of which will be confirmed by the outcome of the appeal process. Hence, the same is to be disclosed as contingent liability.


           

On the legal notice of ₹ 300 lakhs, since the legal opinion states that probability of a cash outflow is more likely than not, it is not a contingent liability but is a provision to be accounted for in the financial statements.


           

**5.4 Option (B)** A patent provides legally enforceable protection for a specified period, which may enable an organisation to protect its innovation and derive economic benefits from it; however, such protection by itself does not necessarily ensure sustainable competitive advantage.


           

**Reason:** A patent grants the holder legally enforceable exclusive rights over an invention for a limited period, which can restrict imitation and allow the firm to capture economic benefits from its innovation. However, a patent does not automatically guarantee sustainable competitive advantage, since competitors may develop substitutes or alternative technologies, the commercial value of the invention may decline, and patent protection eventually expires.


           

**5.5 Option (A)** Incorrect since it is a financial asset/ contractual asset.


           

**Reason:** As per Ind AS 109 on Financial Instruments, an entity shall recognize a loss allowance for credit loss on the following:


           

- A financial asset that is recognized at amortized cost.


           

- A financial asset that is measured at fair value through other comprehensive income.


           

- A lease receivable.


           

- A contract asset or a loan commitment


           

- A financial guarantee contract.


           

Retention money receivable would normally meet the definition of a financial asset or a contract asset based on facts and circumstances applicable to a contract. Accordingly, ECL would be applicable for retention receivables under Ind AS 109.


           

| II. | Answers to the Descriptive Questions |
| --- | --- |


           

**5.6.** To investigate the profitability of the business for judging the accuracy of the schedule of repayment furnished by the borrower, as well as the value of the security in the form of assets of the business already possessed and those which will be created out of the loan, the investigating accountant should take the under-mentioned steps:


           

(1) Prepare a condensed income statement from the Statement of **Profit and Loss for the previous five years**, showing separately therein various items of **income and expenses, the amounts of gross and net profits earned and taxes paid** annually during each of the five years. The amount of maintainable profits determined on the basis of foregoing statement should be increased by the amount by which these would increase on the investment of borrowed funds.


           

(2) Compute the under-mentioned ratios separately and then include them in the statement to show the trend as well as changes that have taken place in the financial position of the company:


           

(i) Sales to Average Inventories held.


           

(ii) Sales to Fixed Assets.


           

(iii) Equity to Fixed Assets.


           

(iv) Current Assets to Current Liabilities.


           

(v) Quick Assets (the current assets that are readily realizable) to Quick Liabilities.


           

(vi) Equity to Long Term Loans.


           

(vii) Sales to Book Debts.


           

(viii) Return on Capital Employed.


           

(3) Enter in a separate part of the statement the break-up of annual sales product-wise to show their trend.


           

**5.7** In respect of tips collected by the company from the guests and distributed to the employees, the person responsible for paying the employee was not the employer at all, but **a third person, namely the guest**. The payments of collected tips included and paid by way of credit cards, UPI or Net Banking in the bills by guest, would not be **payments made “by or on behalf of” an employer**.


           

The contract of employment not being the proximate cause for the receipt of tips by the employee from a guest, such **payments would be outside the scope of Sections 15 and 17** of the Income tax Act, 1961.


           

There is no employer-employee relationship between customers and the employees of Nahar Hotels and Resorts Ltd. and therefore, **such payments do not fall in the nature of salary**. This view is supported by Supreme Court judgment (ITC Ltd v. CIT (2016) 384 ITR 14 (SC).


           

On account of such tips being received from guests and not from the employer, Section 192 of the Income tax Act, 1961, would not get attracted at all in the hands of Nahar


           

Hotels and Resorts Ltd. Thus, the company is **not responsible for deducting tax at source from disbursement of tips to its employees**.


           

**5.8 Evaluation of NHR’s Financial Performance**


           

The benchmark WACC that NHR’s management wants to maintain is below 10%. The company’s actual WACC is 7.636%. NHR has managed to maintain its WACC below the required benchmark primarily on account of its capital structure. Long term debt of ₹ 16 crores, which is the cheaper source of capital, makes up more than half of the total capital employed of ₹ 25 crores.


           

NHR’s financial performance reflects a strong operational foundation, though its capital structure presents certain financial risks that require careful management.


           

With 64% of its capital sourced from debt financing, NHR carries a significant financial obligation in the form of ₹ 1.12 crores in interest payments. While leverage can enhance returns, it also increases financial risk, making strong cash flow management essential for ensuring timely debt repayment and mitigating the risk of financial distress.


           

Despite this high debt level, NHR has demonstrated strong operational efficiency, achieving an PBIT of ₹ 9 crores. This indicates the company’s ability to generate substantial earnings before financial obligations. Additionally, its EVA of ₹ 4.391 crores shows that NHR is earning returns above its cost of capital, confirming that it is creating value for shareholders rather than merely covering financing costs.


           

To sustain this positive path, NHR must carefully assess new investment opportunities, ensuring they generate returns exceeding its benchmark 10% WACC to drive long-term value creation. Moreover, effective risk management strategies—such as hedging against interest rate fluctuations, optimizing capital allocation, and maintaining a financial buffer—will be crucial in mitigating potential risks and ensuring financial stability.


           

Overall, NHR’s strong operational performance and positive EVA highlight its ability to generate value. However, its high reliance on debt necessitates vigilant financial management. To ensure sustainable growth and maximize shareholder value, NHR should focus on prudent debt management, strategic investment in high-return projects, and robust risk mitigation strategies to navigate potential financial challenges effectively.


           

**Workings**


           

| EVA | = | NOPAT – WACC × Capital Employed |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | = | ₹ 6.3 Cr. – 7.636% × ₹ 25 Cr. |
|  | = | ₹ 4.391 Cr. |
| Capital Employed | = | ₹ 5 Cr. + ₹ 4 Cr. + ₹ 16 Cr. |
|  | = | ₹ 25 Cr. |
| WACC | = | (5 + 4)/25 × 12.5% + 16/25 × 4.9% |
|  | = | 7.636% |
| NOPAT | = | [PBIT- Interest - Tax] + Interest (net of tax) |


           **
           

| ₹ in Cr. |  |
| --- | --- |
| PBIT | 9.000 |
| Less: Interest | (1.120) |
| PBT | 7.880 |
| Less: Tax @ 30% | (2.364) |
| PAT | 5.516 |
| Add: Interest (net of tax) [1.12 × (1 - 0.30)] | 0.784 |
| NOPAT | 6.300 |

question:
| Heritage Tea Processing Limited (HTPL) is an unlisted company founded in 1980 under the visionary leadership of Shri Bal Krishnan. The company is headquartered in Bengaluru, Karnataka. The Heritage Tea Group was founded on the belief that tea has the power to dissolve differences, foster connection and bring people together. Now 'Chai pe Charcha' has become a normal phenomenon. The company owns several tea estates in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. Initially focused solely on tea leaf production until 1990, as the popularity of the beverage grew, HTPL decided to broaden its business operations. While maintaining its plantation activities, the company expanded into tea blending, packaging and marketing to strengthen its market presence. Some estates of the company initially operated on plucking cycles of up to 10 days, instead of the ideal 5-6 days. This resulted in coarser leaves, lower out-turn ratios and higher factory rejection rates. Additionally, logistical inefficiencies, such as uncoordinated inter-estate dispatches and underutilized vehicles, led to increased idle hours and higher operational costs. Following a comprehensive cost rationalization and benchmarking exercise, the company standardized plucking cycles by implementing weekly schedules. Today, over 80% of estates maintain the optimal 5-6 days cycle. Logistic optimization measures, including clustered routing and shared vehicle usage, have further reduced idle time and optimized fuel costs. Currently, the company operates a fully integrated tea blending and packaging operation, where at every stage, from tasting and quality inspection to blending and final packing is meticulously managed to ensure purity and preserve its aroma. HTPL's integrated tea manufacturing begins with sourcing high-quality tea leaves, both from its own plantations and selected suppliers in Sri Lanka. Each estate owned by HTPL is overseen by a superintendent and organized into divisions responsible for crop planting, manpower management and operations. Tea plucking is primarily manual, scheduled according to leaf maturity, rainfall and bush type. Harvested leaves are transported to the estate's CTC (Crush-Tear-Curl) or modern processing facilities, where maintaining leaf quality is critical to ensure consistent flavour and overall product quality. At the factory, tea leaves undergo primary processing, including withering, rolling, oxidation or fermentation, drying and grading, to produce tea with desired characteristics. Processed tea is then blended and packaged in retail or bulk formats, often using sustainable packaging solutions. The company distributes finished products via internal channels, wholesalers, retailers, direct-to-consumer outlets and international markets, offering pack sizes from 100 grams to 10 kilograms. Its customers include supermarkets, hotels and restaurants. Marketing and sales efforts, supported by feedback mechanisms, helps refine product quality and service. Sustainability practices are integrated throughout, converting by-products into compost, bio-energy, or secondary products, reducing environmental impact and enhancing brand reputation. The company has transitioned towards renewable energy by installing solar panels at its manufacturing units, significantly reducing reliance on conventional power sources and lowering its carbon footprint. These green energy initiatives generate approximately 30 lakh units of solar power annually, offsetting nearly 2,000 sustainability, the company integrates modern technology with environmentally responsible practices. Around 55-60% of finished products are packaged in recycled bags, supporting resource efficiency. Additionally, tea dust and other organic waste from processing are used as natural fertilisers, improving soil health and minimizing landfill waste. The entry of new suppliers into the tea business is a major cause of concern for the company. These new players are intensifying competition, particularly on pricing. However, the company holds a strong competitive advantage through its superior product quality, state-of-the-art infrastructure and a robust research and development team that continuously introduces innovative tea flavour. The company offers personalized service to customers through dedicated order support, while actively collecting customer feedback via surveys and quality monitoring to refine its blends. Responding to changing consumer preferences and growing health consciousness, the company has expanded its product line since 2020 to include premium blends, organic teas and green tea, receiving a positive market response. The Company's Board reflects a strong commitment to diversity through a balanced and independent composition. It includes an appropriate mix of Executive, Non-Executive and Independent Directors, each selected for their expertise and experience to enhance effective oversight and organizational performance. Mr. G. Krishnan has been serving as Chairman and Managing Director since 2010. With three manufacturing plants, one in Tamil Nadu and two in Karnataka, the Company has a strong presence in both domestic and international markets, offering over 180 Stock Keeping Units (SKUs) and enjoying recognition in more than 50 countries worldwide. Total employee strength at all the manufacturing facilities is 1,500. The company has state-of-the-art machinery installed at each of its tea manufacturing and packing plants. Mr. G. Krishnan attended an international business workshop in Mumbai, where successful business founders and CEOs from around the world shared practical insights on decision-making, business modelling and growth strategies. During the workshop, he attended a lecture by a renowned strategic analyst on the Business Model Canvas, which illustrated how it helps businesses map, design and develop robust models while addressing critical areas for success. Upon returning to the office, Mr. G. Krishnan shared his workshop experience at the Board meeting, highlighting key insights, innovative strategies and actionable recommendations and expressed his intention to develop the company's business model canvas to further streamline operations and identify growth opportunities. Unfortunately, a fire broke out at the Company's factory located in Kodagu, Karnataka on 5th August 2025, resulting in damage to inventories, machinery and equipment. Stock with a total cost of ₹ 1.20 crore was affected and damaged. Company has claimed ITC of ₹ 9.60 lakh on damaged stock in GSTR 3B filed for the month of July 2025. The damaged stock comprised raw materials, packing materials and finished goods, including bulk tea bags and retail cartons ready for dispatch. Machinery and equipment (15% Block) purchased on 1st February 2022 for ₹ 1.77 crore (exclusive of 18% IGST), were completely destroyed in the fire. The company has in place a reinstatement insurance policy covering loss or damage to its building, machinery and inventories due to fire. Against the loss of stock, the Company received insurance compensation of 1.05 crore and against the loss of machinery, it received ₹ 1.40 crore on 30th November 2025. In addition, the Company received equipment from the insurance company with a market value of 0.10 crore as compensation for the equipment destroyed by the fire and the same was put to use on 30th November 2025. HTPL is maintaining a Tea Development Account with NABARD as per the scheme approved by Tea Board. The Written Down Value (WDV) of the machinery and equipment block (Rate of Depreciation: 15%) as per the Income-tax Act, 1961 is ₹ 120 crore as at 1st April 2025. Company placed an order for new machinery and equipment (15% Block) costing ₹ 2.50 crore on 10th August 2025 by withdrawing ₹ 5 crore from the Tea Development Account. HTPL made payment of ₹ 2.50 crore for the new machinery and equipment ordered on 10th August 2025, ₹ 0.05 crore for freight and installation charges, ₹ 0.50 crore spent on office furnishing and renovation (including computers for ₹ 0.25 crore installed in office) and ₹ 1.90 crore on installation of solar panels for use in the factory and plantation estates and the balance amount was not used. The machinery and equipment were installed and put to use on 15th November 2025. HTPL sold a parcel of land in November 2025 for ₹ 3 crore. The land had originally been acquired in January 2023 for ₹ 1.50 crore using funds withdrawn from the Tea Development Account, which were intended for the upgradation of the existing infrastructure of the company's unit. However, the company utilized these funds to purchase the land with the objective of constructing a warehouse, The proposed warehouse could not be developed due to the failure to obtain the necessary approvals from the local government authorities. HTPL held 82% of the shares as at 1st April 2025 of ABC Valley Tea Limited, an unlisted public company engaged in tea manufacturing and trading, with the remaining 18% held by various minority shareholders, including individuals and institutional investors. Over a period of six months, HTPL gradually increased its stake, raising its holding to 91% of the total issued equity share capital by 30th September 2025. In October 2025, HTPL notified ABC Valley Tea Limited of its intention to acquire the remaining 9% of shares. Management of ABC Valley Tea Limited appointed a registered valuer to determine the fair value, who determined the price at ₹ 180 per share. However, the highest price paid by HTPL for any shares acquired in the preceding 12 months was ₹ 170 per share. A notice was sent to 30 minority shareholders. Out of these, 10 shareholders, collectively holding 78% of the minority shareholding entered into separate negotiations with HTPL, which agreed to acquire their shares at ₹ 190 per share, a price higher than the initially determined amount. The remaining 20 shareholders, representing the balance 22% of minority shares, were willing to sell at the original determined price. At present, all packing materials are sourced from external suppliers. In response to the increasing demand for tea sachets and to ensure full control over their quality, shape and size, the management has decided to manufacture sachets in-house. Accordingly, an order was placed on 1st November 2025 for two customised tea sachet forming machines with CNC system and PLC controls (15% Block) from XYZ GmbH situated in Germany at a FOB price of Euro 15,000 each to be despatched in first week of February 2026. The contract includes a price variation clause, under which the price of the machine will increase by 50% of the increase in material cost, if such increase of material cost exceeds 5%. Full payment will be made on or before 31st January 2026 before the despatch of machine. The Finance Manager is considering various hedging strategies to mitigate currency risk in the current volatile foreign exchange environment. As of 1st November 2025, the spot exchange rate stands at ₹ 102 per Euro, with the three-month forward rate at ₹ 104 per Euro. Borrowing rates are 6% in Germany and 10% in India, while deposit rates are 4% and 7%, respectively. Additionally, the German branch of an Indian bank has offered credit at 6% per annum against the opening of an irrevocable letter of credit. Commission charges for issuance of letter of credit are at 2% per annum. The company currently utilizes cash credit and term loan facilities from its bank at an interest rate of 10% per annum. Interest is compounded monthly for borrowings and quarterly for deposits. The Finance Manager assigned CA. Arvind, newly appointed in the Finance Department with expertise in foreign exchange risk management, to analyse the exposure and recommend the most cost-effective hedging strategy. Based on his analysis, the company implemented the recommended hedge to manage its currency exchange risk. Owing to a global rise in steel prices, XYZ GmbH increased the FOB price of the tea sachet forming machine by 3% over the previously agreed price. The Finance Manager received the email notification regarding the price revision on 25th January 2026 and the payment was made on 31st January 2026 in Euros, which were purchased in accordance with the hedging option selected by him. Exchange rate prescribed by RBI as on 31st January 2026 was ₹ 107 per Euro and exchange rate notified by CBIC was ₹ 106 per Euro. XYZ GmbH dispatched the machine by ship on 2nd February 2026. The ship carrying the machine arrived at Cochin Port on 6th March 2026 and the Bill of Entry was filed on 4th March 2026. Freight charges from Germany to India totalled Euro 5,000 and insurance charges of Euro 400 were paid on 31 January 2026. HTPL paid a commission of ₹ 1,61,300 to the local agent in India of the XYZ GmbH. Freight charges of ₹ 1,05,850 were paid to a local transport company for transporting the machine from Cochin Port to the factory situated at Kodagu, Karnataka. The machine was installed and put to use from 25th March 2026. The exchange rate notified by CBIC on the date of the Bill of Entry (04.03.2026) was ₹ 109 per Euro, while on the date of the ship's entry (06.03.2026) it was ₹ 108 per Euro. The Basic Customs Duty rate was 15% on the date of the Bill of Entry but was reduced to 10% with effect from 5th March 2026. The Social Welfare Surcharge is levied at 10% and the Integrated Tax (IGST) under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 is 18%. As part of its Corporate Social Responsibility obligations under the Companies Act, 2013, the Company purchased and distributed 2,000 educational kits comprising school bags, notebooks and stationery items to government schools in a rural area. In addition, the Company donated 250 Tablets to students of Government Aided Schools. The educational kits were procured in February 2026 from a local registered supplier for a total consideration of ₹ 12,90,000, inclusive of GST amounting to ₹ 90,000. The Tablets were purchased from a local registered supplier for ₹ 23,60,000, inclusive of GST amounting to ₹ 3,60,000. The Company claimed the input tax credit (ITC) of the GST paid on these purchases in its GSTR-3B return for the month of February 2026. The Chief Accountant of the Company, not being well-versed in the provisions and technical intricacies of Income Tax, GST and Customs law, engaged the services of CA. Abhinav, having vast experience in tax matters, to determine the correct amount of customs duty payable as well as correct admissibility or reversal of GST input tax credit (ITC) for the year and the depreciation allowable in accordance the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961. CA. Anmol is the Engagement Partner for the statutory audit of the company for the year 2025-26. During the pre-audit meeting, he discussed with the audit team the use of statistical sampling techniques and external confirmation procedures to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence. He decided to apply the stratified sampling method for selecting debtors and creditors. Accordingly, he provided a list of 100 debtors and 80 creditors to the Chief Accountant for sending positive balance confirmation requests, instructing that responses should be sent directly to the auditor's official email ID. While reviewing the list submitted by CA. Anmol, the Chief Accountant identified 6 creditors with zero balances and suggested that confirmations either need not be sent to them or that negative balance confirmations could be sent. However, CA. Anmol directed that confirmation emails be sent to all selected parties as originally planned. Within seven days, confirmation responses were received from 90 debtors and 74 creditors. Out of these confirmations received, 5 debtors' confirmations and 4 creditors' confirmations were not received from the registered email IDs on record and balance confirmations of 10 debtors and 6 creditors with zero balance were not obtained. Upon inquiry, the Chief Accountant informed CA. Anmol that physical letters had already been obtained from those debtors and creditors. During this review, Dinesh, a member of the audit team, observed that in the case of 4 creditors with zero balance, there were high volume transactions and nearly 15% of these transactions had been settled in cash. **1.6 Business Model Canvas given by Osterwalder:**


            

**Key Partners:** Key Partnerships include domestic and international tea leaf suppliers to ensure flexible and reliable sourcing beyond owned estates; sustainable and recycled packaging vendors to support environmental commitments; external logistics providers to strengthen distribution capacity; research institutes and consultants to advance flavor innovation, soil health, and sustainable practices; and government that offer renewable energy incentives and sustainability certifications.


            

These collaborations enhance sourcing ability, reduce operational bottlenecks, strengthen sustainability performance, and improve brand credibility among eco-conscious consumers.


            

**Key Activities:** It includes tea cultivation (plucking, crop planning, workforce management, and leaf quality control) and processing (withering, rolling, fermentation, drying, grading. blending, and packaging). Operations are strengthened by efficient logistics and distribution through coordinated dispatches and optimized routing. Ongoing R&D ensures new flavor development, blend testing, and consistent quality, while sustainability efforts focus on waste conversion, solar energy, and eco-friendly packaging.


            

Standardized plucking cycles and efficient logistics reduce costs and improve productivity, and ongoing R&D strengthens product differentiation and competitive advantage.


            

**Key Resources:** It includes high-quality tea estates, efficient modern processing facilities, skilled human capital, sustainability infrastructure, and strong brand assets with proprietary blends and certifications.


            

Optimizing estate and factory operations reduces waste and rejection rates, while continued investment in R&D and sustainability strengthens brand equity and global competitiveness.


            

**Customer Relationships:** It focuses on delivering personalized service to customers responsive order support, while also engaging direct consumers via loyalty programs that encourage repeat purchases. The company leverages customer feedback through surveys and quality monitoring to continuously refine its blends.


            

Strong relationships with B2B and retail partners improve demand forecasting and inventory optimization, while feedback-driven R&D minimizes product rejection rates and enhances overall quality.


            

**Customer Segments:** HTPL serves diverse customers through internal channels, wholesalers, retailers, direct-to-consumer outlets, and international markets. Its clients include domestic consumers, retail and wholesale buyers, clients like hotels, export customers, and eco-conscious consumers. The company focuses on high value and international segments to boost margins and diversify revenue.


            

By segmenting its customers effectively, HTPL can tailor packaging sizes ranging from 100 g to 10 kg. implement differentiated pricing strategies and design targeted marketing campaigns. Furthermore, focusing on high-value and international segments provides opportunities to expand profit margins and diversify revenue streams, supporting long-term operational growth.


            

**Channels:** The company reaches customers through multiple channels, including company-owned retail stores, wholesalers and distributors across urban and rural areas and partnerships with overseas retailers for exports.


            

Operationally, clustering distribution routes and sharing logistics help reduce costs, while brand awareness enhances margins.


            

**Cost Structure:** This includes variable costs such as labor for plucking and factory operations, raw materials, packaging, logistics, and utilities, alongside fixed costs like estate maintenance, factory depreciation, R&D, marketing, and solar infrastructure. Sustainability investments cover solar panels, waste management systems, recycled packaging, and energy efficiency initiatives.


            

Operational efficiencies through estate benchmarking and optimized logistics reduce idle hours and fuel expenses, enabling competitive pricing against new market entrants without compromising quality.


            

**Revenue Stream:** The business generates revenue through multiple streams, including retail sales of packaged tea (wholesale and B2B supply to hotels, restaurants, and shops, as well as exports to international and specialty markets. Additional income comes from value-added offerings such as premium blends, organic teas, and eco-friendly packaging.


            

This diversified approach reduces reliance on any single market while premium and export products provide higher-margin growth opportunities.


            

**Value Proposition:** HTPL stands out by offering high-quality tea, carefully sourced and processed for consistent purity, aroma, and flavour. Its integrated operations from plantation to packaging ensure strict quality control, while sustainability initiatives like solar-powered factories, recycled packaging, and waste-to-compost programs appeal to eco-conscious consumers. The company also emphasizes product variety and innovation through unique blends developed via R&D, supported by reliable supply through efficient logistics and standardized plucking cycles.


            

These strengths in quality, sustainability, and innovation enable differentiation in a crowded market and create opportunities for premium pricing.

The Business Model Canvas (BMC) helps a company understand how different parts of the business work together to create value, improve efficiency and identify growth opportunities. Based on the insights gained by Mr. G. Krishnan during the international workshop, HTPL can use the Business Model Canvas to strengthen its operations, improve customer satisfaction and support long-term sustainable growth.


            

**1. Key Partners, Key Activities and Key Resources**


            

**Key Partners:** HTPL’s important partners include tea leaf suppliers from Sri Lanka, wholesalers, retailers, supermarkets, hotels, restaurants, logistics providers and sustainable packaging suppliers. The company also works with renewable energy solution providers for solar power generation. These partnerships help the company maintain quality standards, ensure smooth supply chain operations and strengthen market reach.


            

The decision to manufacture tea sachets in-house instead of depending completely on external suppliers would further improve control over quality, size and design of sachets. This can reduce dependency on outside vendors and improve operational efficiency.


            

**Key Activities:** The key activities of HTPL include tea cultivation, manual tea plucking, tea processing, blending, quality testing, packaging, distribution, marketing and customer feedback analysis. Sustainability activities such as solar power generation, use of recycled packaging and converting tea waste into fertilisers are also important operational activities.


            

The company has already streamlined operations by standardizing plucking cycles and improving logistics through clustered routing and shared vehicle usage. These measures have reduced idle time, improved leaf quality and lowered operational costs.


            

**Key Resources:** HTPL’s major resources include its tea estates, manufacturing plants, skilled workforce, research and development team, strong brand reputation and global distribution network. The company’s renewable energy infrastructure is also valuable resource.


            

Its strong research and development capabilities help in introducing innovative tea flavours and premium products such as organic and green tea, which support future growth opportunities.


            

**2. Customer Relationships:** HTPL focuses strongly on maintaining long-term relationships with customers through dedicated order support and regular customer feedback systems. The company continuously monitors customer preferences and uses surveys and quality checks to improve its tea blends and services.


            

By offering consistent product quality, personalized support and innovative tea products, HTPL builds customer trust and loyalty. Expansion into premium tea, organic tea and health-focused products also helps the company meet changing consumer preferences and strengthen customer relationships.


            

The company’s sustainability initiatives and CSR activities further improve brand image and customer goodwill, especially among environmentally conscious consumers.


            

**3. Customer Segments:** HTPL serves multiple customer segments in both domestic and international markets. These include:


            
              
- 
                

Retail customers purchasing packaged tea products


              
              
- 
                

Supermarkets and retail chains


              
              
- 
                

Hotels and restaurants


              
              
- 
                

International buyers across more than 50 countries


              
              
- 
                

Health-conscious consumers preferring organic and green tea


              
              
- 
                

Bulk buyers purchasing large packaging sizes


              
            
            

By offering in different pack sizes ranging from 100 grams to 10 kilograms, HTPL is able to cater to different customer needs and preferences.


            

The growing demand for premium blends, herbal tea and health-oriented tea products provides additional growth opportunities for the company in both Indian and international markets.


            

**4. Cost Structure:** HTPL’s major costs include plantation expenses, labour costs for manual plucking, manufacturing costs, packaging expenses, transportation and logistics costs, research and development expenses and marketing costs.


            

Earlier, the company faced higher operational costs due to longer plucking cycles and inefficient transportation systems. However, standardization of plucking schedules and logistics optimization have helped reduce idle time, improve productivity and lower fuel costs.


            

The installation of solar panels has reduced electricity expenses and dependence on conventional energy sources. Similarly, use of recycled packaging materials and conversion of tea waste into fertilisers reduce waste management costs and support cost efficiency.


            

The decision to manufacture sachets internally may initially require investment in machinery and setup costs, but in the long run it can reduce procurement costs and improve quality control.


            

**5. Value Proposition:** HTPL’s main value proposition lies in providing high-quality tea products with consistent taste, purity and aroma. The company differentiates itself through premium quality tea leaves, modern processing facilities, innovative tea blends and sustainable business practices.


            

Its strong focus on quality control at every stage from tea plucking to blending and packaging helps maintain customer trust and brand reputation. The company also creates value through personalized customer service, environmentally responsible operations and continuous product innovation.


            

The introduction of premium blends, organic tea and green tea allows HTPL to meet changing customer preferences and growing health consciousness. Sustainability initiatives such as renewable energy usage, recycled packaging and waste recycling further strengthen the company’s value proposition and enhance its image as an environmentally responsible brand.


            

**Overall, by developing a clear Business Model Canvas, HTPL can better understand its strengths, improve operational coordination, reduce inefficiencies and identify future growth opportunities in both domestic and global tea markets.**
